newsitem.title: UK: EMU non-participants unlikely to be downgraded - S&P.
newsitem.headline: EMU non-participants unlikely to be downgraded - S&P.

text.p: Sovereign and corporate ratings of countries that are not part of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) are unlikely to be automatically downgraded, a director of Standard & Poor's (S&P) told a news conference on Monday.

"We do not see any corporate actions based solely on this issue," said Konrad Reuss, director at S&P. "Just because you are in or you are out will not be sufficient reason. Sovereign ratings of the "outs' initially won't change."
He said many companies, such as pharmaceuticals, would be affected in only a minor way by EMU, since they already operate on a global basis.
Reuss said the focus of S&P's analysis of countries within EMU would change to reflect the fact that the onus of monetary policy will be shifted to the European Central Bank.
"Individual countries' fiscal and economic policies will be much more important," said Reuss. "They will be viewed as regional governments are today."
He said the emphasis the rating agency will place on domestic governance will outweigh the effect of any "creative accounting" employed by governments in order to meet the Maastricht criteria.
Reuss said pension liabilities were likely to be central to analysis of European Union countries, as they all faced the same problem of an ageing population paying into a pay-as-you-go scheme.
"We will continue to monitor the situation," he said. "We will consider whether a government is committed to addressing the problem."
He noted that one of the reasons for Italy's downgrade in 1994 was its failure to make sufficient progress towards pension reform.
"We would like to see progress on pensions this millenium, for the problems which must be faced in the opening decades of the next," said Reuss.
